summary:
Huellas Espaciales is a bilingual educational website that brings to life the stories of spacecraft and equipment left on the Moon and Mars. We built it for school-age children and space enthusiasts who want to discover what these machines accomplished and where they ended up.

Young Explorers can follow animated mission stories, earn coins in a quiz, and explore Mars in a 3D expedition. Space Enthusiasts can explore maps and mission profiles and compare three documented orbital encounters in Space Scrapper, from a collision to an avoidance maneuver.

We used NASA’s Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) to document the Apollo lunar rover and identify Cosmos 2361, NASA/JPL observations to explain Opportunity’s evidence of ancient water, and NASA reports to explain orbital collision risk. By connecting real mission records with interactive stories, Huellas Espaciales helps learners understand what these machines taught us and why what we leave in space matters.
details:
How the project works

Huellas Espaciales is an interactive website in English and Spanish that tells the stories of machines left on the Moon and Mars. Visitors choose between two routes designed for different audiences.

In Young Explorers, spacecraft and rovers tell their own stories through short animated scenes. Children can examine Apollo 17’s orange soil, see an astronaut retrieve Surveyor 3’s camera, earn coins in a quiz, and explore Mars in a separate 3D expedition. The activities identify fictional scenes and connect them to real missions.

In Space Enthusiasts, visitors explore maps, photographs, and profiles of six lunar and Martian missions. The Space Scrapper section compares three documented orbital encounters: a collision, a close pass, and an avoidance maneuver. Visitors can sort the cases by date or estimated separation and see how forecasts compare with what happened.

Data and technology

We used NASA’s Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) to document the Apollo lunar rover and identify Cosmos 2361. NASA/JPL mission records and photographs support the stories, and NASA’s Conjunction Assessment Risk Analysis resources help explain orbital collision risk.

We built the website with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and used Node.js for local testing. The Mars Heritage expedition uses Three.js for 3D rendering. ChatGPT and Codex assisted with writing, translation, and website development. Google Gemini helped create the 3D game.

Why it matters

We designed the experience for phones and computers, with short activities for younger readers and more technical detail for enthusiasts. By connecting real mission records with interactive stories, we aim to help learners understand what these machines taught us, where they ended up, and why tracking objects left in orbit matters.
